first_impression.reaction: My assistant shortlisted it because we want to marry legally and Greece is on the list. The first screen gives a straight answer, 'Yes', with a date and the law, and no rainbow fuss or cheerleading. Calm and factual is what I want. Her summary: legal since February 2024, civil only, the municipality sets the paperwork, recognised in Australia, and Mykonos and Santorini are safer bets. I read the safety section, the venue questions and the close myself. The document lists and embassy hours are for the family office.

journey.quote: Yes. As at November 2026, same-sex marriage in Greece is legal: Greek law allows a civil marriage between two persons of different or the same sex, and the change has been in force since 16 February 2024.
journey.reaction: Answers the question in the first word. No tiptoeing, no celebration. That reads as people who know what they're doing.

journey.section: Is same-sex marriage legal in Greece?
journey.quote: Its circular confirms that a marriage between two persons of the same sex is valid in the Greek legal order and is entered in the civil registry like any other marriage.
journey.reaction: Reassuring legally. But 'entered in the civil registry' is exactly where my mind goes next: who can see that record? For us, given where part of the family lives, that matters more than the ceremony.

journey.section: Civil ceremony at the town hall
journey.quote: On Rhodes, the Town Hall ceremony takes place every Wednesday and Friday, two adult witnesses over 18 must be present, and the couple returns to the registry office the next working day to sign and have the marriage certificate drawn up.
journey.reaction: Clear, and useful for the timeline. But a town hall on a set weekday, then walking back into a public office the next morning, is the opposite of private. I need to know the registrar can come to us.

journey.section: Civil ceremony at the town hall
journey.quote: Build your timeline around the registry, not the venue.
journey.reaction: Good advice, stated once, no padding. My family office will appreciate the order of operations.

journey.quote: Every notarial service needs an appointment, Monday to Friday, 9:00am to 12:30pm, though apostille and CNI documents can be submitted by post.
journey.reaction: Accurate, but this is for my assistant, not me. The whole document section is long for a first read; she skimmed it into three lines.

journey.section: What the law covers, and what it does not
journey.quote: Couples declare their future children's surname before the wedding, to a notary or to the officiant, who must ask for it.
journey.reaction: I would never have known this, and in our families a surname is not a small thing. This is the kind of detail that makes me think they've actually looked.

journey.section: Is Greece LGBT friendly for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Avoid public displays of affection, especially in rural areas.
journey.reaction: Honest, and I'd rather they quote the government than pretend. It also tells me why we need a closed property and our own security, not a village square.

journey.section: Is Greece LGBT friendly for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Share that advice with your guests along with the itinerary.
journey.reaction: Fine for guests, but for 250 people it is not enough to send a link. I want to hear how they would protect the guests on the ground. That isn't on the page.

journey.quote: In Rhodes City they include Rodini park and the Town Hall's central entrance staircase.
journey.reaction: A park and the town hall steps. Pretty for some couples, but a public staircase is a photograph on a stranger's phone. I skipped the rest of the Rhodes list.

journey.quote: How private is the ceremony space, and can we take the whole venue or a section of it?
journey.reaction: Yes. That is my first question, and it is in their list. The best line on the page for me.

journey.quote: Have you hosted same-sex weddings before, and will you put that in writing?
journey.reaction: Sharp. A venue that hesitates here would hesitate with my guests too. I'd add: and can you keep it off your social media.

journey.section: Legal ceremony, symbolic celebration or both
journey.quote: Some couples keep the civil ceremony small, with the two witnesses and close family, and hold the larger celebration that evening or the next day.
journey.reaction: This is probably us: a very small legal moment, then the real celebration. Good to see it framed as normal rather than second best.

journey.section: Plan your Greece wedding with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: The registrar settles the marriage. Everything around it, from the island and the venue to your guests' rooms and the long dinner after, is ours to plan.
journey.reaction: Understated and confident. It doesn't oversell, which I respect.

unanswered_questions: Can the registrar perform the civil ceremony privately at a venue we have taken over, rather than at the town hall or a public municipal location?
Is the Greek civil registry entry or the marriage certificate publicly searchable, and can anything be done to keep it out of view?
Can a property on Mykonos or Santorini be closed to the public for the wedding and the days around it, and can our own security work with the venue's?
Have they planned a same-sex wedding in Greece at 200 or more guests, and how do they handle guest safety and discretion on the ground?
Does the Australian route still apply if one of us lives in Dubai, and who do we speak to first?
Is there a private or referral route to someone senior rather than a web form?
would_share_with: My assistant and family office, for the Rhodes document list, the CNI from Athens and the surname declaration
My partner, for the three ways to shape the day and the safety section

cta_reaction.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, and confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
cta_reaction.why: Quiet and sensible, and 'anywhere in the world' suits a family across Dubai, Sydney and London. But nothing here speaks to discretion or scale, which are the two reasons I'd hire anyone, and I don't fill in web forms. Through my assistant or a referral, possibly.

top_3_changes: Next to the town hall section or in 'Questions to ask a venue', add a question about whether the registrar can officiate privately at the venue and who will be present, so a reader who needs discretion sees the private route acknowledged without new claims.
Add one privacy question to the venue list, such as whether the venue will keep the wedding off its own social media and how it manages guest and outside photography.

In the safety section, after 'Share that advice with your guests', add a short line pointing couples to ask venues about private transfers and on-site security for guests, phrased as questions to ask rather than promises.
